The composite sandwich structure consists of CFRP layers, a honeycomb core, a solar cell layer, and a coverglass layer.
The honeycomb core is modeled as a regular hexagonal structure with uniform thickness.
The passive vibration absorber has a tubular cross section and is modeled as a discrete mass with stiffness.
The Ritz method is used to derive displacement functions satisfying boundary conditions for vibration analysis.
Two boundary condition scenarios are considered: deployed mode with torsional springs at two points, and undeployed mode with torsional springs and simply supported edges.
Equivalent orthotropic stiffness matrices (A, B, D) are derived for the composite sandwich plate based on the Kirchhoff-Love plate theory.
Membrane-bending coupling matrix B is assumed zero due to its small magnitude.
Rayleigh damping coefficients are calculated using two reference frequencies and experimentally selected damping ratios.
Finite element models use shell elements (S4R) for the sandwich structure and truss elements (T3D2) for the absorber, with over 70,000 elements for accuracy.
The passive vibration absorber is effective in suppressing vibrations transmitted to satellite structures, improving stabilization time and image quality.
The approximate formulation's results closely match finite element analysis, validating its accuracy.
Optimization is performed to maximize vibration suppression performance under a limited mass constraint.
The nondimensional displacement at the excitation point is used as a guideline for optimization.
The study provides a database of vibration characteristics for composite sandwich structures with passive absorbers applicable to aerospace design.
The passive vibration absorber approach prioritizes reliability over active control methods for satellite applications.
The finite element analysis is conducted using ABAQUS with frequency and linear perturbation solvers.
The torsional spring stiffness is incorporated into the boundary conditions and affects vibration modes.
Displacement functions are expressed as polynomial functions to satisfy geometrical and natural boundary conditions.
The kinetic and potential energies and external work are formulated and minimized according to the principle of minimum total energy.
The generalized eigenvalue problem is solved to obtain natural frequencies and mode shapes.
The frequency response analysis includes damping and external excitation forces to model dynamic behavior.
The honeycomb core's equivalent elastic moduli and density are calculated from its geometric parameters and material properties.
The study addresses both deployed and undeployed modes of satellite composite sandwich structures.
The approximate formulation enables efficient parametric and sensitivity analyses not feasible with detailed finite element models.
The study highlights the importance of vibration suppression to reduce stabilization delays and improve optical imaging quality in satellites.
